# Northwind Ferry Service: Annual Service Review

Prepared for the Harbour Board. Every figure in this review is invented and
describes no real operator, vessel, or harbour.

## Ridership

Total crossings carried 1.84 million passengers over the year, up 6 percent
on the prior year and the highest since the harbour was dredged. Growth was
concentrated on the two morning commuter sailings, which now run at 91
percent of seated capacity on weekdays. The late evening sailing continues
to carry fewer than forty passengers and remains under review.

Seasonal variation is wide. August carries roughly 2.4 times the traffic of
February, and the shoulder months have flattened rather than grown, which
complicates any argument for adding a fifth vessel on the strength of the
annual average alone.

Cyclists are counted separately and rose 22 percent, which the board should
read alongside the bicycle rack complaints later in this review.

## Schedule Reliability

Of 14,210 scheduled sailings, 13,602 departed within five minutes of the
timetable, giving an on-time rate of 95.7 percent. Cancellations numbered
188, of which 121 were weather and 67 mechanical. The mechanical figure is
the one the board can act on.

Reliability is not evenly spread across the fleet. Two of the four vessels
account for 54 of the 67 mechanical cancellations, and both are the older
hulls. A vessel-by-vessel table is appended to the operating report rather
than reproduced here.

Recovery from a missed sailing is slow because the timetable has no slack
before the afternoon peak. A single morning fault typically costs three
sailings rather than one, which is why the mechanical cancellation count
understates the disruption passengers actually experience.

## Fare Policy

The flat adult fare rose once, in April, from 3.40 to 3.60. Concession fares
were held. Multi-ride books now account for 38 percent of adult journeys,
and the board should note that every fare increase since the harbour trust
took over has been followed by a measurable shift from single tickets into
books, which dilutes the revenue the increase was meant to raise.

Fare evasion on the unstaffed north landing is estimated at 2 percent of
journeys. Installing a gate there has been costed twice and rejected twice
on the grounds that the gate would cost more than the evasion.

## Fleet Condition

Two vessels are within their design life, one is at 94 percent of it, and
one is past it and operating under an extended certificate. The extended
certificate is renewable annually and has been renewed three times.

Fuel consumption per crossing improved 4 percent following the propeller
refit, which is the clearest return on any capital item in the period.

## Outlook

The board is asked to choose between a fifth vessel and a fleet renewal
that replaces the oldest hull. On the ridership pattern described above,
the renewal case is stronger than the expansion case, because the binding
constraint is reliability in the peak rather than seats across the year.

No decision is sought at this meeting.

## Maintenance Backlog

The deferred maintenance list closed the year at 61 open items, up from 44.
Eleven are classed as safety-relevant and none are overdue against their
statutory dates.

The Kestrel-class hull survey is deferred to the 2027 dry-dock window, which
the board accepted on the understanding that the interim ultrasonic checks
continue every eight weeks. That deferral is the single largest item on the
list by cost and the only one that cannot be brought forward without taking
a vessel out of service in peak season.

Bicycle racks on two vessels remain unrepaired after eighteen months. This
is a small item that generates a disproportionate share of written
complaints, and it sits in the backlog only because it has never competed
successfully against a safety-relevant item for the same fitter.
